newsitem.title: GREECE: Greenpeace urges Greece to change energy policy.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace urges Greece to change energy policy.

text.p: Greenpeace urged Greece on Wednesday to change its wasteful energy policies to avoid disastrous climate changes and a depletion of its precious water reserves.

The sunny Mediterranean country could see its climate changed drastically by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, Stelios Psomas, director of the international organisation's Greek office, told a news conference.
"Although it urges other countries to commit to reducing dangerous pollutants, Greece has asked to be allowed to increase its own. This is unacceptable and hypocritical," he said.
Greenpeace painted a dark picture of Greece's climate in the future unless the country adopted much more ambitious targets for cutting carbon dioxide emissions by conserving energy.
Global warming would eliminate 85 percent of Greek wetlands, rainfall would decline by 10-30 percent by 2030 and the tourist island of Crete would face acute water problems by 2010, Psomas said.
Rain would come increasingly in the form of sporadic and disastrous storms, and agricultural output would decrease by about 35 percent, he added.

Greenpeace has compiled scientific studies on climate change in the Mediterranean to push for big, legally binding reductions in greenhouse gases at a summit of industrialised nations in Kyoto, Japan in December.
The environmental group wants pollutants produced by burning fossil fuel to be cut by 20 percent by 2005, 40 percent by 2010 and 50 percent by 2020.
The European Union has made the most advanced proposal in international negotiations so far, asking for a phased reduction of 15 percent by 2015, Psomas said.
"Obviously this is not enough but what is more interesting is that Greece has asked to increase its emissions by 30 percent by 2010 in the name of development," he said.
Per capita carbon dioxide emissions in Greece are double the world average at nine tonnes annually because of wasteful attitudes, Psomas said.

"Possibilities for energy conservation in industry, homes and transport are so great that we could meet very high standards for climate protection if we honestly tried," he said. "Asking for a 30 percent increase means doing nothing for the next 13 years."
